question: ChemKing uses a standard costing system in the manufacture of its single product. The 35,000 units of raw material in inventory were purchased for $105,000, and two units of raw material are required to produce one unit of final product. In November, the company produced 12,000 units of product. The standard cost for material allowed for the output was $60,000, and there was an unfavorable quantity variance of $2,500. The materials price variance for the units used in November was

options.A: $2,500 unfavorable.
options.B: $12,000 unfavorable.
options.C: $12,500 unfavorable.
options.D: $6,000 unfavorable.

correctExplanation: The formula for calculating the materials price variance is (AP − SP) × AQ. The actual price for raw materials was $105,000 ÷ 35,000 units in inventory, or $3.00 per unit. The standard price is $2.50 per unit of raw materials, calculated as ($60,000 ÷ 12,000 units actually produced) ÷ 2 units of materials per unit produced. The Actual Quantity in the formula is the actual quantity of the raw materials that were used in producing the 12,000 finished units. It is not the actual quantity of product produced, nor is it the standard quantity of materials for the actual quantity produced. So to calculate the price variance, we need to know how many units of materials were actually used in production, and the question does not tell us that. However, it does tell us that there was an unfavorable quantity variance. So to figure out how many units of materials were actually used, we first have to work out the quantity variance, which the question says is an unfavorable $2,500, to solve for the AQ in that formula. The quantity variance formula is (AQ − SQ) × SP. Since the question tells us that the materials standard is two units of raw materials for each unit produced, we know that the standard quantity of materials for 12,000 units was 24,000 units. The actual quantity we do not know yet. The standard price was $2.50 per unit of raw material ($60,000 standard allowed ÷ 12,000 units actually produced ÷ 2 units of materials per unit produced). Therefore, our formula is: (AQ − 24,000) × 2.50 = 2,500 Solving for AQ, we get AQ = 25,000, as follows: 2.5AQ − 60,000 = 2,500 2.5AQ = 62,500 AQ = 25,000 Now, we can put the actual quantity of materials used into the materials price variance formula and calculate the materials price variance. (AP − SP) × AQ ($3.00 − $2.50) × 25,000 = $12,500 Unfavorable

explanations.A: $2,500 Unfavorable is the quantity variance, which is given in the question.
explanations.B: This answer results from using the standard amount of materials for the actual quantity produced as the AQ in the materials price variance formula, instead of the actual quantity of materials used. See the correct answer for a complete explanation.
explanations.D: This answer results from using the actual quantity of units produced as the AQ in the materials price variance formula, instead of the actual quantity of materials used. See the correct answer for a complete explanation.

question: A company established its annual direct material budget to produce 300,000 units as follows. 150,000 pounds of material @ $0.75 per pound = $112,500 Throughout the year, the company produced 310,000 units of finished goods using 0.48 pounds per unit at a cost of $0.76 per pound. The direct material efficiency variance is

options.A: $900 favorable.
options.B: $588 unfavorable.
options.C: $4,650 favorable.
options.D: $1,488 unfavorable.

correctExplanation: The direct materials efficiency variance is a quantity variance. The formula for a quantity variance is (AQ – SQ) × SP. The AQ is the actual quantity of materials used for the actual production. The SQ is the standard quantity of materials allowed for the actual production. The SP is the standard price per unit of direct materials. The actual quantity of direct materials used is 310,000 × 0.48, or 148,800. The standard quantity of materials allowed for the actual production is calculated as follows. 150,000 pounds of material ÷ 300,000 units budgeted = 0.50 pounds of material per unit produced. Since 310,000 units were produced, the material allowed for the actual production was 0.50 × 310,000, or 155,000 pounds. The standard price is $0.75 per pound. The direct materials efficiency variance is therefore (148,800 – 155,000) × $0.75 = $(4,650). Because it is a negative amount for a cost variance, it is a favorable variance.

explanations.A: This is the actual quantity of direct materials used for the actual production minus the budgeted quantity of direct materials allowed for the budgeted production, the difference multiplied by the standard price per unit of direct materials. The SQ used in the formula for the direct materials efficiency variance needs to be the standard quantity of materials allowed for the actual production.
explanations.B: This is the difference between the actual cost to produce 310,000 units and the budgeted cost to produce 300,000 units. The budgeted cost for 300,000 units is the master budget amount. The direct material efficiency variance is calculated using the flexible budget amount, or the budgeted cost allowed for the actual production.
explanations.D: This is the price variance. The formula for the direct materials efficiency variance, a quantity variance, is (AQ – SQ) × SP. The AQ is the actual quantity of materials used for the actual production. The SQ is the standard quantity of materials allowed for the actual production. The SP is the standard price per unit of direct materials.

question: A favorable materials price variance coupled with an unfavorable materials usage variance would most likely result from

options.A: Machine efficiency problems.
options.B: The purchase and use of higher than standard quality materials.
options.C: The purchase of lower than standard quality materials.
options.D: Product mix production changes.

correctExplanation: The favorable materials price variance means that the material was purchased for a lower price than planned. This could happen due to a lower skill level of workers, poor material quality or some other reason. However, these two variances together are most likely caused by the same reason. question: The controller for Durham Skates is reviewing the production cost report for July. An analysis of direct materials costs reflects an unfavorable flexible budget variance of $25. The plant manager believes this is excellent performance on a flexible budget for 5,000 units of direct materials. However, the production supervisor is not pleased with this result because he claims to have saved $1,200 in materials cost on actual production using 4,900 units of direct materials. The standard materials cost is $12 per unit. Actual materials used for the month amounted to $60,025. The actual average cost per unit for materials was
correctExplanation: Actual materials used for the month amounted to $60,025, and 4,900 units of direct materials were used. The actual average cost per unit of material was $12.25 ($60,025 ÷ 4,900).

explanations.A: This answer results from using the Price Variance formula to calculate the value of AP in the formula but using the total flexible budget variance of $25 on the right side of the equation. The $25 variance given in the problem is called the flexible budget variance. Since it is not called either the price variance or the quantity variance, the $25 variance is the total flexible budget variance which incorporates both the price and the quantity variances. It is incorrect to use the Price Variance formula at all to find the answer to this question, because the Price Variance is not given in the question and thus is unknown. Since the correct amount for the right side of the equation is unknown, there is no way to properly use the Price Variance formula to calculate the value of AP. The answer to the question is simply the total actual cost divided by the actual amount used. That answer is what would be used as the AP in the Price Variance formula.
explanations.B: This answer results from using the Price Variance formula to calculate the value of AP in the formula but reversing the favorable-unfavorable result in the formula: (AP − 12) × 4,900 = 1,200 AP = 12.244898 The value of AP is the correct answer to this question. However, $12.244898 is not the value of AP. The variance of $(1,200) favorable that the production supervisor is claiming would need to be a negative amount in the formula above, since it is a favorable variance. However, when the value of AP is calculated using a negative amount for the 1,200, the result is AP = $11.755, which is not one of the answer choices. Therefore, using the Price Variance formula to calculate the value of AP, using 1,200 or even (1,200) for the variance, must be incorrect. The Price Variance formula cannot be used to calculate the value of AP because the Price Variance is not given in the problem. The value of AP (the actual average price) and the correct answer to this question is simply the actual cost divided by the actual amount used. When the correct value of AP is used in the Price Variance formula, the Price Variance that results is $1,225 unfavorable. The $(1,200) favorable variance that the production supervisor is claiming is actually the materials Quantity Variance. The Quantity Variance formula cannot be used to find the value of AP, since AP is not used in the Quantity Variance formula. The Price Variance of $1,225 unfavorable combined with the Quantity Variance of $(1,200) favorable equals the total flexible budget variance as calculated by the controller of $25 unfavorable.
explanations.D: This is standard cost per unit of material, not the actual average cost per unit of material. See the correct answer for a complete explanation.

question: Tower Company planned to produce 3,000 units of its single product, Titactium, during November. The standard specifications for one unit of Titactium include 6 pounds of materials at $0.30 per pound. Actual production in November was 3,100 units of Titactium. The accountant computed a favorable materials purchase price variance of $380 and an unfavorable materials quantity variance of $120. Based on these variances, one could conclude that

options.A: The actual usage of materials was less than the standard allowed.
options.B: More materials were used than were purchased.
options.C: The actual cost of materials was less than the standard cost.
options.D: More materials were purchased than were used.

correctExplanation: A favorable materials purchase price variance indicates that the actual price paid for the direct materials was less than the standard price.

explanations.A: An unfavorable materials quantity variance of $120 indicates that more materials were used than the standard allowed, not less.
explanations.B: A difference between the quantity of materials purchased and used has nothing to do with a favorable materials purchase price variance of $380 and an unfavorable materials quantity variance of $120. The materials efficiency variance is the difference between the actual quantity of material used and the standard quantity of materials allowed multiplied by the standard price. The materials purchase price variance uses the actual quantity of materials purchased instead of the quantity of materials used.
explanations.D: A difference between the quantity of materials purchased and used has nothing to do with a favorable materials purchase price variance of $380 and an unfavorable materials quantity variance of $120. The materials efficiency variance is the difference between the actual quantity of material used and the standard quantity of material allowed for the actual output, multiplied by the standard price. table: 3 lbs. of direct materials @ $4 per lb.

Sterling is very unhappy about the situation and is preparing to reply to the memorandum explaining the reasons for his dissatisfaction. All of the following are valid reasons for Sterling’s dissatisfaction except that the

options.A: cause of the unfavorable material usage variance was the acquisition of substandard material.
options.B: the variance shown on the accounting department's report as the materials price variance is incorrect because it is actually the total materials variance; and the materials price variance is actually favorable, not unfavorable.
options.C: variance calculations fail to properly reflect that actual production exceeded normal production capacity.
options.D: standards have not been adjusted to the engineering changes.

correctExplanation: This is not a valid reason for Sterling's dissatisfaction. The standard usage of 3,000 lbs. is the standard quantity of 3 lbs. of direct materials per unit multiplied by the 1,000 units actually produced. Thus the standard usage used in the materials quantity variance does reflect the fact that actual production exceeded the 900 units that is the normal production capacity.

explanations.A: This is a valid reason for Sterling's dissatisfaction. If the raw material was, in fact, substandard, that could easily cause an unfavorable material usage variance. The quality of the raw materials purchased is primarily the responsibility of the purchasing department. It is not the responsibility of the production department.
explanations.B: This is a true statement and is a valid reason for Sterling's dissatisfaction. The report from the accounting department is incorrect. The correct calculation of the materials price variance is (AP − SP) × AQ. The actual price for the materials used was $12,600 ÷ 3,300 pounds, or $3.8181 per pound. Thus the correct materials price variance was (3.8181 − 4) × 3,300, or $(600) favorable, not unfavorable as is shown on the accounting department's report. The quantity variance is (AQ − SQ) × SP, or (3,300 − 3,000) × 4, which equals $1,200 unfavorable. The quantity variance should be expressed in monetary terms, not in units (pounds in this situation) of direct materials as in the question. The total materials variance is the combination of the price variance of $(600) favorable and the quantity variance of $1,200 unfavorable, which equals $600 unfavorable. Thus the accounting department's report is presenting the total materials variance and calling it the materials price variance. The accounting department's report does not present the materials price variance at all. If the report did show the correct materials price variance, that variance, as calculated above, would be $(600) favorable, not $600 unfavorable.
explanations.D: This is a valid reason for Sterling's dissatisfaction. If engineering changes have been made and the standards have not been changed, that could cause a material usage variance. The production department is not responsible for setting standards and maintaining them.

question: The following is a standard cost variance analysis report on direct labor cost for a division of a manufacturing company. Job Actual Hours at Actual Wages Actual Hours at Standard Wages Standard Hours at Standard Wages 213 $ 3,243 $ 3,700 $ 3,100 215 15,345 15,675 15,000 217 6,754 7,000 6,600 219 19,788 18,755 19,250 221 3,370 3,470 2,650 Totals $48,500 $48,600 $46,600 What is the total flexible budget direct labor variance for the division?
intro: The following is a standard cost variance analysis report on direct labor cost for a division of a manufacturing company. Job Actual Hours at Actual Wages Actual Hours at Standard Wages Standard Hours at Standard Wages
tail: What is the total flexible budget direct labor variance for the division?

options.A: $100 favorable.
options.B: $2,000 unfavorable.
options.C: $1,900 favorable.
options.D: $1,900 unfavorable.

correctExplanation: This question is asking for the total flexible budget direct labor variance. The total flexible budget variance is the difference between the actual cost and the total flexible budget amount. The total flexible budget amount for direct labor is the total standard cost for the actual level of output—which is the standard hours at standard wages, or the standard number of hours allowed for the actual production at the standard wage rate allowed per hour. The total flexible budget amount in this question is in Column 3, titled “Standard Hours at Standard Wages." Column 3 contains the total standard cost for the standard hours allowed for the actual output at the rate of the standard wages allowed per hour. Therefore, the total flexible budget direct labor variance is the difference between the total line from Column 1 ($48,500)—the total actual cost—and the total line from Column 3 ($46,600)—the total standard cost for the actual production, or the total flexible budget amount. Since the actual cost ($48,500) is $1,900 greater than the flexible budget amount ($46,600), the variance is $1,900 unfavorable. Note: The direct labor efficiency variance is the difference between the total "Actual Hours at Standard Wages" and the total "Standard Hours at Standard Wages," which is $48,600 − $46,600 = $2,000 Unfavorable. The direct labor rate variance is the difference between the total "Actual Hours at Actual Wages" and the total "Actual Hours at Standard Wages," which is $48,500 − $48,600 = $(100) Favorable. The total direct labor variance, which is also called the flexible budget direct labor variance, is the combination of the direct labor efficiency variance and the direct labor rate variance. Combining $2,000 U and $(100) F gives us the total direct labor variance (the flexible budget direct labor variance) of $1,900 U, which is the answer to the question.

explanations.A: This is the direct labor rate variance, a price variance. The direct labor rate variance is the difference between the Actual Hours at Actual Wages and Actual Hours at Standard Wages. The direct labor rate variance is one component of the total flexible budget direct labor variance. The other component is the direct labor efficiency variance. However, the question asks for the total flexible budget direct labor variance, which is the total of the direct labor efficiency variance and the direct labor rate variance.
explanations.B: This is the direct labor efficiency variance, a quantity variance. The direct labor efficiency variance is the difference between the Actual Hours at Standard Wages and the Standard Hours at Standard Wages. The direct labor efficiency variance is one component of the total flexible budget direct labor variance. The other component is the direct labor rate variance. However, the question asks for the total flexible budget direct labor variance, which is the total of the direct labor efficiency variance and the direct labor rate variance.
explanations.C: The flexible budget variance is unfavorable, because the actual cost incurred is greater than the standard cost for the actual level of output (the flexible budget)

studyUnit: Study Unit 3: C.1. Direct Labor Variances

question: Of the following pairs of variances found in a flexible budget report, which pair is most likely to be related?

options.A: Labor efficiency variance and fixed overhead volume variance.
options.B: Labor rate variance and variable overhead efficiency variance.
options.C: Material price variance and variable overhead efficiency variance.
options.D: Material usage variance and labor efficiency variance.

correctExplanation: A material usage variance can be caused by labor factors, and a labor efficiency variance can be caused by material quality factors. If employees are new or untrained, an unfavorable labor efficiency variance can result. The untrained employees may also cause more direct material spoilage, which will result in an unfavorable material usage variance. It can work the other way, as well. Knowledgeable and efficient employees can create both a favorable labor efficiency variance and a favorable material usage variance. Furthermore, an unfavorable material usage variance can be caused by inferior materials. The inferior materials that the employees have to work with can also cause an unfavorable labor efficiency variance as well, because it may take longer to produce the product using inferior materials.

explanations.A: It is not likely that a labor efficiency variance and a fixed overhead volume variance would be related. A labor efficiency variance results from a difference between the actual number of labor hours required for the actual output and the standard number of labor hours allowed for the actual output. The fixed overhead volume variance (also called the fixed overhead production-volume variance) is a measure of capacity utilization. It is caused by the actual production level being different from the production level used to calculate the budgeted fixed overhead rate. The labor efficiency variance and the fixed overhead volume variance are not related, and it is very unlikely that one would cause the other.
explanations.B: It is not likely that a labor rate variance and a variable overhead efficiency variance would be related. A labor rate variance results from a difference between the actual hourly rate paid for direct labor used and the budgeted hourly rate. The variable overhead efficiency variance is the amount of the total variance caused by a different usage of the allocation base (either direct labor hours or machine hours) than was expected. Even if direct labor hours are being used as the allocation base, the usage of the allocation base is a quantity variance whereas the labor rate variance is a price variance. The labor rate variance and the variable overhead efficiency variance are not related, and it is very unlikely that one would cause the other.

A material price variance results from a difference between the actual price per unit of the direct materials used and the budgeted price per unit. question: Under a standard cost system, labor price variances are usually not attributable to

options.A: Union contracts approved before the budgeting cycle.
options.B: Labor rate predictions.
options.C: The assignment of different skill levels of workers than planned.
options.D: The use of a single average standard rate.

correctExplanation: The labor price or rate variance is calculated as: (Actual Rate − Standard Rate) × Actual Hours. The only figure union contracts can influence is the actual labor rate. The standard rate is set by the budget at the beginning of the year. As union contracts are approved before the budgeting cycle begins, the information about potential changes in wages and salaries is already included in the budget and standards. Therefore, a union contract approved before the budgeting cycle cannot be the cause of a labor rate variance.

explanations.B: As with all future predictions, labor rate predictions can have inaccuracies. If the standard labor rate was set using these predicted numbers, it may cause a labor rate variance.
explanations.C: The assignment of different skill levels of workers than was planned in most cases will cause a labor price variances. The labor rate variance is calculated as: (Actual Rate − Standard Rate) × Actual Hours. When there is a difference between the rates of assigned (with lower or higher working skills) and planned workers, a labor rate variance will most likely occur.
explanations.D: If the standard labor rate was set using a single average standard rate, it may cause a labor rate variance. If the rate doesn't reflect the proportion of hours worked of each wage rate group of workers, a variance will result.

question: A company budgets to produce 4,000 units of its product. Actual production is 4,200 units. Which one of the following is closest to the actual hourly rate for direct labor if the total direct labor flexible-budget variance was an unfavorable variance of $4,400?
correctExplanation: The solution to this is a three-step process. Step 1: Calculate the direct labor rate variance. The direct labor flexible-budget variance is the combination of the direct labor rate variance and the direct labor efficiency variance. The direct labor efficiency variance was $8,600 unfavorable and the direct labor flexible-budget variance (the total of the rate variance and efficiency variance) was $4,400 unfavorable. Therefore, the direct labor rate variance was the difference between them: $4,400 U − $8,600 U = ($4,200) F. Step 2: Use the direct labor efficiency variance formula to find the value of AQ (the actual quantity, the number of direct labor hours actually used): (AQ − SQ) × SP = Efficiency (Quantity) Variance (AQ − 4,200) × 43 = 8,600 Divide both sides of the equation by 43: AQ − 4,200 = 200 Add 4,200 to both sides of the equation: AQ = 4,400 Step 3: Use the direct labor rate variance formula with $43 (given) as SP, the direct labor standard rate per hour, 4,400 (calculated in Step 2) as AQ and ($4,200) as the variance (calculated in Step 1) to find the value of AP: (AP − SP) × AQ = Rate Variance (AP − 43) × 4,400 = (4,200) Divide both sides of the equation by 4,400: AP − 43 = (0.955) Add 43 to both sides of the equation: AP = 42.045

Step 2: Use the direct labor efficiency variance formula to find the value of AQ, the actual quantity of DL hours used. This step was done correctly and resulted in the correct actual quantity of DL hours used: 4,400. Step 3: Use the direct labor rate variance formula to find the value of the actual wage rate. The DL rate variance formula results in the DL rate variance, which was calculated incorrectly in Step 1 and so was used incorrectly in this step. But in addition to using the wrong rate variance, the sign of the rate variance used here did not match the variance calculated in Step 1. The variance calculated in Step 1 was unfavorable, but a negative $13,000 variance is used on the right side of the equals sign in this step, which for a cost item signifies a favorable variance. If the correct variance of $4,200 favorable--as a negative number--had been used on the right side of the equation, the answer would have been calculated correctly.

studyUnit: Study Unit 3: C.1. Direct Labor Variances

question: A company has a direct labor price variance that is favorable. Of the following the most serious concern the company may have about this variance is that

options.A: the production manager may not be using human resources as efficiently as possible.
options.B: actual production is less than budgeted production.
options.C: the circumstances giving rise to the favorable variance will not continue in the future.
options.D: the cause of the favorable variance may result in other larger unfavorable variances in the value chain.

correctExplanation: A company’s "value chain" is its chain of activities for transforming inputs into the outputs that customers value. This process of transformation includes all of the primary activities (business functions) that add value to the product or service, as well as support activities. It involves functions from R&D through production to marketing and sales, and on to customer service, including the activities that play supporting roles such as information systems, materials management, and human resources. When a company has a favorable labor price (rate) variance, it is because the company has paid hourly wage rates that are lower than the standard wage rates. Usually, that occurs when the company has employed workers who are less qualified than the workers the company's management expected to have. Use of less qualified workers can lead to a higher probability that the products produced and sold will be of lower quality and have more defects. Lower quality products and higher defective rates will lead to increased costs for customer service, as the customers who buy the products will have more difficulty with them. It can also lead to higher warranty costs, because more products will need to be repaired or replaced for customers during the warranty period. The amount gained from the favorable labor price variance, and possibly even more, may be lost through greater unfavorable variances in labor and material usage further down the value chain.

explanations.A: The labor efficiency variance measures whether human resources are being used efficiently. The labor price (rate) variance does not.
explanations.B: A direct labor price variance is not caused by actual production volume being less than budgeted production volume.
explanations.C: There is no reason to believe that circumstances giving rise to the favorable variance will not continue in the future.

question: The budgeted output for the month of May was for 9,000 units with direct material at $15 per unit. Direct labor was budgeted at 45 minutes per unit for a total of $81,000. Actual output for the month was 8,500 units with $127,500 in direct material and $77,775 in direct labor expense. The direct labor standard of 45 minutes was maintained throughout the month. Variance analysis of the performance for the month of May would show a(n)

options.A: Favorable direct labor efficiency variance of $1,275.
options.B: Unfavorable direct labor price variance of $1,275.
options.C: Unfavorable direct labor efficiency variance of $1,275.
options.D: Favorable material usage variance of $7,500.

correctExplanation: The direct labor price variance is calculated (AP − SP) × AQ or (Actual Rate − Standard Rate) × Actual Hours. The standard labor rate per hour is $12, calculated as follows: the labor standard is 45 minutes per unit, or 0.75 of an hour. 9,000 units were planned, so total planned hours was 0.75 × 9,000 or 6,750 hours. Total planned cost was $81,000, so the standard cost per hour was $81,000 ÷ 6,750 hours, or $12 per hour. The actual labor rate was $12.20, calculated as follows: The labor standard of 45 minutes per unit or 0.75 of an hour per unit was maintained. 8,500 units were actually produced, so the total actual hours was 0.75 × 8,500 or 6,375 hours. Total actual cost was $77,775, so the actual cost per hour (the actual rate) was $77,775 ÷ 6,375 hours, or $12.20 per hour. Putting the numbers into the formula, we get ($12.20 − $12.00) × 6,375 = $1,275 Unfavorable.

explanations.A: Because the problem states that the direct labor standard was maintained throughout the period, the direct labor efficiency variance must be zero, not $1,275 Favorable.
explanations.C: This is the direct labor price variance. Because the problem states that the direct labor standard was maintained throughout the period, the direct labor efficiency variance must be zero, not $1,275 Unfavorable.
explanations.D: This is (9,000 × $15) − $127,500, which is not a material usage variance. 9,000 is the budgeted output, and budgeted output is not used in calculating manufacturing input variances.

question: A manager prepared the following table by which to analyze labor costs for the month: Actual Hours at Actual Rate Actual Hours at Standard Rate Standard Hours at Standard Rate $10,000 $9,800 $8,820 What variance was $980?

options.A: Labor rate variance.
options.B: Labor efficiency variance.
options.C: Volume variance.
options.D: Labor spending variance.

correctExplanation: To solve this question, we need to calculate all the suggested variances possible from this set of data. It's better to start with most simple ones. The labor efficiency variance is: (Actual Hours − Standard Hours for Actual Output) × Standard Rate, or (Actual Hours × Standard Rate) − (Standard Hours for Actual Output × Standard Rate). The actual hours times the standard rate is $9,800. The standard hours times the standard rate is $8,820. The difference is $980 unfavorable.

explanations.A: To solve this question, we need to calculate all the suggested variances possible from this set of data. It's better to start with most simple ones. The labor rate variance is: (Actual Rate − Standard Rate) × Actual Hours or (Actual Rate × Actual Hours) − (Standard Rate × Actual Hours). The actual rate times the actual hours is $10,000. The standard rate times the actual hours is $9,800. The difference is $200 unfavorable. This is not the result we are looking for.
explanations.C: The volume variance is related to the fixed overhead and is the difference between the budgeted amount of fixed overhead and the amount of fixed overhead applied (standard rate × standard input for the actual level of output). The volume variance cannot be determined using the given set of data.
explanations.D: There is no such thing as a labor spending variance. Labor variances are either labor efficiency variances or labor rate variances. The variable overhead spending variance is related to variable overhead and is the difference between the actual application rate and the standard application rate multiplied by the actual quantity of the application base (level of activity). This can also be calculated as the actual variable overhead incurred − (the actual usage of the application base × the standard variable overhead rate). This cannot be determined using the given set of data.

question: MinnOil performs oil changes and other minor maintenance services (e.g., tire pressure checks) for cars. The company advertises that all services are completed within 15 minutes for each service. On a recent Saturday, 160 cars were serviced resulting in the following labor variances: rate, $19 unfavorable; efficiency, $14 favorable. If MinnOil's standard labor rate is $7 per hour, determine the actual wage rate per hour and the actual hours worked.

options.B: Wage Rate $6.67/hour, Hours Worked 42.71.
options.C: Wage Rate $7.45/hour, Hours Worked 42.00.
options.D: Wage Rate $6.55/hour; Hours Worked 42.00.

correctExplanation: This is an example of price and quantity variances applied to a service business. To answer this question, we must work out both the price (rate) variance and the quantity (efficiency) variance. The price variance formula is (AP − SP) × AQ = Price Variance. The quantity variance formula is (AQ − SQ) × SP = Quantity Variance. Since these are cost items, a negative variance is a favorable variance (actual is lower than standard) and a positive variance is an unfavorable one (actual is higher than standard). The Standard Quantity (SQ) is the standard for the number of hours to service 160 cars. The standard is 0.25 hours per car multiplied by 160 cars, which is 40 hours. The Standard Price (SP) is given as $7 per hour. The Price Variance is $19 unfavorable. The Quantity Variance is ($14) favorable. Whenever we have all of the values we need except one, we can set up a simple equation and solve for the missing variable. We have all of the values for the Quantity Variance formula except for AQ. So the first equation will be: (AQ − 40) × 7 = (14) 7 AQ − 280 = (14) 7 AQ = 266 AQ = 38, and this is the actual hours worked. Now, we can take that value for AQ and use it in the Price Variance formula to solve for AP: (AP − 7) × 38 = 19 38 AP − 266 = 19 38 AP = 285 AP = 7.50, and this is the actual wage rate.

explanations.B: This answer results from using $19 unfavorable as the Efficiency (Quantity) Variance and $14 favorable as the Rate (Price) Variance. Instead, the Rate Variance is $19 unfavorable and the Efficiency Variance is $14 favorable.
explanations.C: This answer results from solving the Quantity Variance formula for the variable AQ using a positive Quantity Variance in the formula instead of a negative one. The Quantity (Efficiency) Variance is favorable. Since it is a cost, a favorable variance is represented by a negative amount. Therefore, the Quantity Variance used in the formula should be negative. See the correct answer for a complete explanation.
explanations.D: This answer results from two errors: (1) Solving the Quantity Variance formula for the variable AQ using a positive Quantity Variance in the formula instead of a negative one. The Quantity (Efficiency) Variance is favorable. Since it is a cost, a favorable variance is represented by a negative amount. Therefore, the Quantity Variance used in the formula should be negative. (2) Solving the Price Variance formula for the variable AP using a negative Price Variance in the formula instead of a positive one. The Price (Rate) Variance is unfavorable. Since it is a cost, an unfavorable variance is represented by a positive amount. Therefore, the Price Variance used in the formula should be positive. See the correct answer for a complete explanation.

question: The controller of a hotel company has noticed that the payroll expenses of the housekeeping department were unfavorable to the budget even though the rooms occupied were flat to the budget. A further investigation has revealed that the unfavorable payroll variance was due mostly to an unfavorable efficiency variance, partially offset by a favorable rate variance. The pay rates in the housekeeping department are in the following order: manager, supervisor, guest-room attendant, co-op students. There are some dual-rate supervisors in the department who are paid either as supervisors or guest-room attendants depending on their duties on certain days. Which one of the following is a possible explanation for the unfavorable payroll expenses?

options.A: Most of the dual-rate supervisors were scheduled to do the guest-room attendants’ job.

options.C: Most of the dual-rate supervisors were scheduled to do the supervisor’s job.

correctExplanation: If the company hired a greater number of less experienced co-op students and fewer of the more experienced guest-room attendants than budgeted and used the less experienced co-op students in place of some of the more experienced guest-room attendants, that would cause the unfavorable labor efficiency variance. That would change the mix of labor used. The actual ratio of the labor inputs used would be different from the budgeted ratio of labor inputs. As a result, the time the co-op students would require to do the work could easily be extended beyond the estimated time in the budget and cause an unfavorable labor efficiency variance. That would also cause the favorable labor rate variance because more hours would be worked by lower-paid employees and fewer hours would be worked by higher-paid employees than had been budgeted.

The direct material standards for one batch of 100 pounds of the Breakfast Blend are as follows (the standard incorporates some extra material to allow for normal loss in the grinding and mixing process, and thus the number of pounds of the three types of beans sum to more than 100 pounds): Colombian 45 pounds @ $8.00/pound Blue Mountain 32 pounds @ $6.40/pound Kona 26 pounds @ $9.60/pound During November, 10 batches of Breakfast Blend were produced. The actual amount of coffee beans used for the 10 batches and the actual costs per pound were as follows: Actual Cost/Pound Actual Pounds Used for Output
tail: What was the total direct materials variance for Breakfast Blend for the month of November?

options.A: $72 Favorable.
options.B: $301 Unfavorable.
options.C: $47 Unfavorable.
options.D: $119 Favorable.

correctExplanation: The total direct materials variance is the difference between the total actual cost and the total flexible budget standard cost allowed for the actual output. Actual cost: Colombian $8.30 × 470 pounds $ 3,901 Blue Mountain $6.20 × 325 pounds 2,015 Kona $9.80 × 220 pounds 2,156 Total actual cost $8,072 Flexible budget standard cost: Colombian $8.00 × 450 pounds (45 lbs. × 10 batches) $ 3,600 Blue Mountain $6.40 × 320 pounds (32 lbs. × 10 batches) 2,048 Kona $9.60 × 260 pounds (26 lbs. × 10 batches) 2,496 Total standard cost $8,144 The total direct materials variance for the month of November is $8,072 − $8,144 = $(72). Because the variance is negative for a cost variance, actual cost was lower than the standard cost, so the variance is favorable. Note: The total actual and total standard costs can also be calculated on a per batch basis and the total cost per batch multiplied by the 10 batches produced to calculate the total actual and total standard costs.

explanations.B: This answer is the difference between the actual cost for the Colombian beans used and the flexible budget standard cost for the Colombian beans allowed for the actual output. The total direct materials variance is the difference between the total actual cost and the total flexible budget standard cost allowed for the actual output.
explanations.C: This answer is the average actual cost per pound used minus the average standard cost per pound, the difference multiplied by the actual quantity of coffee beans used. The total direct materials variance is the difference between the total actual cost and the total flexible budget standard cost allowed for the actual output.
explanations.D: This answer is the difference between the actual quantity of coffee beans used and the standard quantity of coffee beans allowed for the output, the difference multiplied by the average standard cost per pound. The total direct materials variance is the difference between the total actual cost and the total flexible budget standard cost allowed for the actual output.

question: The efficiency variance for either labor or materials can be divided into

options.A: Volume variance and mix variance.
options.B: Spending variance and yield variance.
options.C: Yield variance and mix variance.
options.D: Yield variance and price variance.

correctExplanation: When more than one input is used for either direct materials or direct labor, the total material quantity (efficiency) or labor efficiency variances can be broken down into two subvariances: the mix and the yield variances. The mix variance is the part of the quantity variance that results because the mix of material actually used was different from the mix that was supposed to have been used. (For example, including more corn and less wheat in the cereal than the standard called for). The yield variance results from the difference between the total quantity of the inputs that were actually used to produce the actual output and the total standard quantity that should have been used to produce the actual output.

explanations.A: The total material quantity (efficiency) and labor efficiency variances can be broken down into the two subvariances, but the volume variance is not one of them.
explanations.B: The total material quantity (efficiency) and labor efficiency variances can be broken down into the two subvariances, but the spending variance is not one of them.
explanations.D: The total material quantity (efficiency) and labor efficiency variances can be broken down into the two subvariances, but the price variance is not one of them.

options.A: $1,050 unfavorable.

correctExplanation: The materials mix variance equals the actual total quantity used multiplied by the difference between the weighted average standard price for the actual mix per unit of direct materials, which in this question is kilograms (waspAM) and the weighted average standard price for the standard mix per kilogram (waspSM). (waspAM − waspSM) × AQ The weighted average total standard price for the actual mix is (21,000 × $0.75) + (14,000 × $0.90) = $28,350, and the weighted average standard price per kilogram for the actual mix (waspAM) is $0.81 ($28,350 ÷ 35,000 kg). The weighted average standard price for the standard mix (waspSM) is $0.80 per kilogram ($240 standard total cost per batch ÷ 300 standard total kg per batch). The mix variance is ($0.81 − $0.80) x 35,000 = $350 Unfavorable.

explanations.A: This answer is calculated as the actual total quantity used multiplied by the difference between the weighted average standard price for the standard mix and the weighted average actual price for the actual mix. The materials mix variance equals the actual total quantity used multiplied by the difference between the weighted average standard price for the actual mix (waspAM) and the weighted average standard price for the standard mix (waspSM): (waspAM − waspSM) × AQ
explanations.B: This answer is calculated as the actual total quantity used multiplied by the difference between the weighted average actual price for the actual mix and the weighted average standard price for the standard mix. The materials mix variance equals the actual total quantity used multiplied by the difference between the weighted average standard price for the actual mix (waspAM) and the weighted average standard price for the standard mix (waspSM): (waspAM − waspSM) × AQ
explanations.D: This calculates the amount of the variance correctly, but the variance is unfavorable.

question: Highlight Inc. uses a standard cost system and applies factory overhead to products on the basis of direct labor hours. If the firm recently reported a favorable direct labor efficiency variance, then the

options.A: direct labor rate variance must be unfavorable.
options.B: variable overhead spending variance must be favorable.
options.C: fixed overhead volume variance must be unfavorable.
options.D: variable overhead efficiency variance must be favorable.

correctExplanation: If the direct labor efficiency variance is favorable, it means the actual quantity of labor used was lower than the standard quantity allowed for the actual output. If variable overhead is applied on the basis of direct labor hours and the direct labor efficiency variance is favorable, then the variable overhead efficiency variance will also be favorable.

explanations.A: The direct labor efficiency variance is (AQ − SQ) × SP, or (AQ × SP) − (SQ × SP). If the variance is favorable, the first number will be lower than the second number and the variance will be negative because AQ is lower than SQ; and it means the actual quantity of labor used was lower than the standard quantity allowed for the actual output. The direct labor rate variance is the price variance for direct labor. The formula is (AP − SP) × AQ, or (AP × AQ) − (SP × AQ). Since these two variances are calculated in completely different ways, there are no grounds for drawing any conclusions about the direct labor rate variance from the direct labor efficiency variance. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.B: The direct labor efficiency variance is (AQ − SQ) × SP, or (AQ × SP) − (SQ × SP). If the variance is favorable, the first number will be lower than the second number and the variance will be negative because AQ is lower than SQ; and it means the actual quantity of labor used was lower than the standard quantity allowed for the actual output. The variable overhead spending variance is actual total variable overhead incurred minus budgeted variable overhead based on inputs actually used. The difference between these two variances is that the second number of the direct labor efficiency variance is (SQ × SP), or the standard cost based on the standard quantity for the actual output, whereas the second number of the variable overhead spending variance is budgeted variable overhead based on inputs actually used (not standard inputs). Since the two formulas are essentially different, no conclusions can be drawn about whether or not a favorable direct labor efficiency variance means the variable overhead spending variance must also be favorable. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: The direct labor efficiency variance is (AQ − SQ) × SP, or (AQ × SP) − (SQ × SP). If the variance is favorable, the first number will be lower than the second number and the variance will be negative because AQ is lower than SQ; and it means the actual quantity of labor used was lower than the standard quantity allowed for the actual output. The fixed overhead production-volume variance is budgeted fixed overheads minus the fixed overhead applied. Since these two variances have no information in common, there are no grounds for drawing any conclusions about the fixed overhead production volume variance from the direct labor efficiency variance.

correctExplanation: The flexible budget overhead variance equals the difference between the total actual overhead incurred and the flexible budget total overhead (variable and fixed). The flexible budget fixed overhead equals the master budget amount of $27,000. The budgeted variable factory overhead rate is $3 per labor hour, the standard hours to produce one unit of product is 3 hours, and 1,650 units were produced. Thus, the flexible budget variable factory overhead was $14,850. The actual overhead costs were $39,930. The total flexible budget fixed and variable factory overhead is $41,850 ($14,850 + $27,000). Therefore, the flexible budget overhead variance is ($1,920) favorable ($39,930 − $41,850). Since the actual overhead is less than the budgeted overhead, the variance is favorable.

question: Water Control Inc. manufactures water pumps and uses a standard cost system. The standard factory overhead costs per water pump are based on direct labor hours and are as follows: Variable overhead (4 hours at $8/hour) - $32 Fixed overhead (4 hours at $5/hour*) - $20 Total overhead cost per unit - $52 * Based on a capacity of 100,000 direct labor hours per month. The variable overhead spending variance for November was

options.A: $40,000 unfavorable.
options.B: $60,000 favorable.
options.C: $12,000 favorable.
options.D: $48,000 unfavorable.

correctExplanation: The variable overhead spending variance is calculated as follows: Actual VOH incurred − Predetermined VOH rate × Actual quantity of VOH allocation base used = Variable OH spending variance All the information needed to answer the question is given in the question. Actual variable overhead incurred was $740,000. The predetermined variable overhead rate was $8 per direct labor hour. The actual quantity of the variable overhead allocation base (direct labor hours) used was 94,000 hours. Variable OH spending variance = $740,000 − ($8 × 94,000) = $(12,000) Favorable

explanations.D: This is the variable overhead efficiency variance. See the correct answer for a complete explanation.

options.A: $96,000 unfavorable.

options.D: $60,000 favorable.

correctExplanation: The variable overhead efficiency variance is calculated as follows: (Actual Activity Level of VOH allocation base used for Actual Output − Standard Activity Level of VOH allocation base allowed for Actual Output) × Standard Application Rate. The actual activity level is 94,000 direct labor hours. The standard activity level is calculated as the standard of 4 hours of direct labor per unit multiplied by the 22,000 units produced during the period, or 88,000 direct labor hours. The standard application rate is $8/hour. Therefore, the variable overhead efficiency variance is (94,000 − 88,000) × $8 = $48,000 Unfavorable. The variance is unfavorable because the actual activity level was greater than the standard activity level.

explanations.B: This is the difference between the actual direct labor costs of $940,000 and the actual variable overhead costs of $740,000, which does not mean anything. See the correct answer for a complete explanation.

question: Water Control Inc. manufactures water pumps and uses a standard cost system. The standard factory overhead costs per water pump are based on direct labor hours and are as follows: Variable overhead (4 hours at $8/hour) - $32 Fixed overhead (4 hours at $5/hour*) - $20 Total overhead cost per unit - $52 * Based on a capacity of 100,000 direct labor hours per month. The following additional information is available for the month of November: 22,000 pumps were produced although 25,000 had been scheduled for production. 94,000 direct labor hours were worked at a total cost of $940,000. The standard direct labor rate is $9 per hour. The standard direct labor time per unit is 4 hours. Variable overhead costs were $740,000. Fixed overhead costs were $540,000. The fixed overhead spending variance for November was:

options.A: $240,000 unfavorable.
options.B: $40,000 unfavorable.
options.C: $70,000 unfavorable.
options.D: $460,000 unfavorable.

correctExplanation: The fixed overhead budget/spending variance is the difference between the actual fixed overhead incurred and the budgeted fixed overhead costs. The actual amount of fixed overhead costs was $540,000. The budgeted amount of fixed overhead was $500,000 ($5 of fixed overhead per labor hour multiplied by 100,000 budgeted labor hours). We use the budgeted amount of labor hours (100,000) because we need to calculate what the total budgeted fixed overhead amount was that the company used in its calculation of the cost per direct labor hour. To calculate the budgeted cost per direct labor hour, the company divided the total budgeted fixed cost by the budgeted number of labor hours. Therefore, to find the budgeted fixed manufacturing cost, we reverse the process and multiply the budgeted cost per labor hour by the number of budgeted labor hours. The amount of budgeted fixed cost is the same for any level of production. Budgeted fixed cost is the same in the flexible budget as it is in the static budget. So in calculating the budgeted fixed manufacturing overhead, it does not matter what the actual level of production was. The fixed overhead budget/spending variance is $40,000 unfavorable ($540,000 − $500,000). The actual fixed overhead costs incurred were higher than the budgeted amount, so the variance is unfavorable.

explanations.A: This amount is the difference between the actual variable overhead and the budgeted fixed overhead. See the correct answer for a complete explanation.
explanations.C: This answer results from using the actual amount of labor hours used (94,000) to calculate the budgeted fixed overhead costs instead of the budgeted labor hours (100,000). We use the budgeted amount of labor hours (100,000) because we need to calculate what the total budgeted fixed overhead amount was that the company used in its calculation of the cost per direct labor hour. To calculate the budgeted cost per direct labor hour, the company divided the total budgeted fixed cost by the budgeted number of labor hours. Therefore, to find the budgeted fixed manufacturing cost, we reverse the process and multiply the budgeted cost per labor hour by the number of budgeted labor hours. The amount of budgeted fixed cost is the same for any level of production. Budgeted fixed cost is the same in the flexible budget as it is in the static budget. So in calculating the budgeted fixed manufacturing overhead, it does not matter what the actual level of production was.
explanations.D: This answer results from two errors: (1) Using $10 per hour as the budgeted fixed overhead application rate instead of the rate of $5 per hour as given in the problem; and (2) Misinterpreting the results of the resulting calculation as an unfavorable variance. The fixed overhead spending variance is actual fixed overhead incurred minus budgeted fixed overhead. Actual fixed overhead incurred is given in the problem as $540,000, but budgeted fixed overhead needs to be calculated. Since fixed overhead does not change with changes in activity (within the relevant range), we can calculate what the budgeted fixed overhead was by multiplying the planned production in units by the planned number of direct labor hours (the application base) per unit and multiplying again by the budgeted fixed overhead application rate per hour allowed of the application base, given in the problem as $5. This answer uses the actual direct labor cost per hour ($10, or $940,000 ÷ 94,000) instead of the budgeted fixed overhead application rate per hour to calculate the budgeted fixed overhead. Using the actual direct labor cost per hour results in a budgeted fixed overhead amount of $1,000,000 (25,000 units budgeted production × 4 hours per unit × $10 per hour). Subtracting $1,000,000 from the actual fixed overhead incurred of $540,000 equals $(460,000). If the budgeted fixed overhead had been calculated correctly and budgeted fixed overhead were really $1,000,000, the fixed overhead spending variance would be a favorable variance, not an unfavorable one, because actual cost would be less than budgeted cost. In calculating all variances except for the fixed overhead production volume variance, we subtract the budgeted amount from the actual amount. A positive number for a cost variance means an unfavorable variance because the actual cost was greater than the budgeted cost. A negative number for a cost variance means a favorable variance because the actual cost was lower than the budgeted cost.

options.A: 100 direct labor hours inefficient.
options.B: 400 direct labor hours inefficient.
options.C: 400 direct labor hours efficient.
options.D: 100 direct labor hours efficient.

correctExplanation: The answer to this question is the Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance divided by the budgeted rate for applying variable manufacturing overhead of $20 per direct labor hour. This will tell us the difference between the actual quantity of direct labor hours used for the actual output and the standard quantity of direct labor hours allowed for the actual output. That, in turn, will tell us how efficient or inefficient the company's use of direct labor was. Another way of looking at it is this: Since (AQ − SQ) × SP equals the Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance, the Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance divided by the standard price ($20) equals the difference between AQ and SQ. And the difference between AQ and SQ is what we need to find to answer the question. The Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance is the difference between the Total Variable Overhead Variance and the Variable Overhead Spending Variance (because the Variable Overhead Spending Variance plus the Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance equals the Total Variable Overhead Variance.) The Total Variable Overhead Variance is equal to actual incurred variable overhead of $80,000 minus flexible budget variable overhead of $90,000, or $(10,000) Favorable. The problem tells us that the Variable Overhead Spending Variance is $(2,000) Favorable. Therefore, the Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance must be $(10,000) minus $(2,000), which is $(8,000) Favorable. The Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance of $(8,000) divided by the budgeted rate for applying variable manufacturing overhead of $20 per direct labor hour equals (400). This means the actual quantity of direct labor hours (AQ) used for the actual output was 400 hours less than the standard quantity of direct labor hours allowed for the actual output (SQ). Thus, Tiny Tykes was 400 hours efficient in its use of direct labor hours.

explanations.A: This is the Variable Overhead Spending Variance divided by the budgeted rate for applying variable manufacturing overhead of $20 per direct labor hour calculated using a positive (unfavorable) variance amount. Since the question is asking about the company's efficiency, the answer to this question is the Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance divided by the budgeted rate for applying variable manufacturing overhead of $20 per direct labor hour. Furthermore, the Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance is a negative (favorable) amount.
explanations.B: This is the Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance divided by the budgeted rate for applying variable manufacturing overhead of $20 per direct labor hour calculated using a positive (unfavorable) variance amount. The Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance is a negative (favorable) amount.
explanations.D: This is the Variable Overhead Spending Variance divided by the budgeted rate for applying variable manufacturing overhead of $20 per direct labor hour. Since the question is asking about the company's efficiency, the answer to this question is the Variable Overhead Efficiency Variance divided by the budgeted rate for applying variable manufacturing overhead of $20 per direct labor hour.

question: Which of these variances is least significant for cost control?

options.A: Fixed O/H volume variance.
options.B: Materials quantity variance.
options.C: Variable O/H spending variance.
options.D: Labor price variance.

correctExplanation: The fixed overhead volume variance is the difference between the budgeted amount of fixed overhead and the amount of fixed overhead applied (standard rate × standard input for the actual level of output). It does not reflect any differences between actual costs and budgeted costs. This variance concerns only the level of production. If the actual level of production is lower than the budgeted level, the fixed overhead volume variance will be unfavorable. If the actual production level is higher than the budgeted level, the fixed overhead volume variance will be favorable. Because this variance arises from a variance in the level of production, it is not very significant for cost control purposes.

explanations.B: The materials quantity variance is the difference between the quantity of materials actually used in production and the standard quantity of materials allowed for the actual level of output. It is an important area of cost control.
explanations.C: The variable overhead spending variance is the difference between the actual application rate (the actual application rate is calculated as the actual overhead costs ÷ the actual usage of the allocation base) and the standard application rate multiplied by the actual quantity of the application base. Because actual variable costs are used in this variance, it is an important area of cost control.
explanations.D: The labor price variance is the difference in labor rates between actual and standard used in production. It is an important area of cost control.

question: Huffman Corporation's budget indicated that it should produce 50,000 units of finished goods, while incurring 20,000 hours of direct labor and $150,000 of variable manufacturing overhead. Huffman actually produced 52,000 finished goods units using 22,000 hours of direct labor and incurring $160,000 of variable manufacturing overhead. If Huffman uses a standard cost system and applies variable manufacturing overhead based on direct labor hours, its variable overhead spending variance was

options.A: $5,000 favorable.
options.B: $4,000 unfavorable.
options.C: $10,000 unfavorable.
options.D: $9,000 unfavorable.

correctExplanation: The variable overhead spending variance is: Total variable overhead actually incurred (AP × AQ) − (Predetermined VOH rate × actual quantity of VOH application base [MH or DLH] used) (SP × AQ) = Variable overhead spending variance Total variable overhead actually incurred is given as $160,000. The predetermined variable overhead rate was $150,000 ÷ 20,000 DLH = $7.50 per DLH. The actual quantity of the VOH application base (DLH) used is given as 22,000 DLH. Therefore, the variable overhead spending variance was $160,000 − ($7.50 × 22,000) = ($5,000) Favorable. The variance is favorable because it is a cost variance and it is negative, meaning the actual cost was lower than the standard cost allowed for the actual output.

Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.

question: A fixed overhead volume variance based on standard direct labor hours measures:

options.A: Fixed overhead efficiency.
options.B: Fixed overhead use.
options.C: Deviation from standard direct labor hour capacity.
options.D: Deviation from the normal, or denominator, level of direct labor hours.

correctExplanation: The fixed overhead volume variance (also called the fixed overhead production-volume variance) is the budgeted amount of fixed overhead (in the static budget) minus the amount of fixed overhead applied (standard rate × standard input for the actual level of output). The budgeted amount of fixed overhead is what was projected as the total amount of fixed overhead to be incurred during the period at the beginning of the year when the budget was developed. Traditionally, overhead is applied to individual products throughout the year using some standard allocation basis, usually direct labor hours, machine hours, materials cost, units of production, or some similar measure that can be measured and calculated. The measure used is called the activity base. A predetermined rate is calculated by dividing the budgeted amount of manufacturing overhead by the budgeted activity level. The budgeted activity level is the number of units of the activity base (labor hours, machine hours, etc.) allowed for the expected production during the coming year. As production continues throughout the year, the amount of the activity base allowed for the amount of product actually produced is multiplied by the predetermined rate to calculate the amount of overhead to be applied. The fixed overhead volume variance is caused by the actual production level being different from the production level (called the denominator level) used to calculate the budgeted fixed overhead rate. If the amount of overhead applied is greater than the budgeted amount, the variance will be favorable because it means that the actual level of production was greater than the budgeted level of production. That is good because it means the facilities are being more fully utilized. If the amount of overhead applied is less than the budgeted overhead, the variance will be unfavorable because it means that actual production was lower than the budgeted production level.

explanations.A: There is no fixed overhead efficiency variance because fixed costs are not related to levels of output and therefore are unable to be used efficiently or inefficiently.
explanations.B: The fixed overhead volume variance does not relate to the fixed overhead usage.
explanations.C: The fixed overhead volume variance does not relate to the capacity of standard direct labor hours. Top of Form

explanations.C: The total fixed overhead variance is not a potential cost reduction that can be achieved from better cost control.

question: Nanjones Company manufactures a line of products distributed nationally through wholesalers. Presented below are planned manufacturing data for the year and actual data for November of the current year. The company applies overhead based on planned machine hours using a predetermined annual rate. Planning Data Annual November Fixed manufacturing overhead $1,200,000 $100,000 Variable manufacturing overhead 2,400,000 220,000 Direct labor hours 48,000 4,000 Machine hours 240,000 22,000 Direct labor hours (actual) 4,200 Direct labor hours (plan based on output) 4,000 Machine hours (actual) 21,600 Machine hours (plan based on output) 21,000 Fixed manufacturing overhead $101,200 Variable manufacturing overhead $214,000 The fixed overhead production-volume variance for November was
intro: Nanjones Company manufactures a line of products distributed nationally through wholesalers. Presented below are planned manufacturing data for the year and actual data for November of the current year. The company applies overhead based on planned machine hours using a predetermined annual rate. Planning Data Annual November
table: Direct labor hours (plan based on output)
tail: The fixed overhead production-volume variance for November was

options.A: $1,200 unfavorable.
options.B: $10,000 favorable.
options.C: $5,000 unfavorable.
options.D: $5,000 favorable.

correctExplanation: The fixed overhead production-volume variance is the difference between the budgeted amount of fixed overhead and the amount of fixed overhead applied (standard rate × standard input for the actual level of output). It is Budgeted Fixed Overhead minus Applied Fixed Overhead. This is the only time for an expense variance calculation that a budgeted cost amount comes before an actual cost amount, and yet a negative amount (actual is higher than budget) is a favorable variance. Nanjones applies overhead based on planned machine hours using a predetermined annual rate. The amount of the planned fixed manufacturing overhead was $1,200,000 and the amount of planned machine hours were 240,000. Thus, the standard application rate for fixed manufacturing overhead was $5 per machine hour ($1,200,000 ÷ 240,000). The number of machine hours allowed for the actual level of output in November was 21,000. Now we can calculate the amount of applied fixed manufacturing overheads as $105,000 ($5 × 21,000). The budgeted amount of fixed manufacturing overhead is the static budget amount planned for November of $100,000, which is the annual amount of $1,200,000 divided by 12. Therefore, the fixed overhead volume variance is: $100,000 − $105,000 = ($5,000) favorable. The fixed overhead production-volume variance is caused by the actual production level being different from the production level used to calculate the budgeted fixed overhead rate. It measures usage of facilities, and so it is not a comparison of actual incurred cost with budgeted cost the way other variances are. When production facilities are used more than was planned (actual is greater than budget), the variance will be favorable because the company has gotten more use from its capacity than it thought it would. When production facilities are used less than was planned (actual is less than budget), the variance is unfavorable because it means the company had unused capacity. The amount of the variance is a rough measure of the cost of the unused capacity. When the company has unused capacity, the cost for that unused capacity should not be passed on to customers in higher prices. Instead, the company should find other uses for the capacity. Management may consider developing a new product to make use of the unused capacity, renting out part of the factory to another company, taking contract work that other companies are outsourcing, or even selling the unused facilities. This variance helps management to see the cost of the unused capacity. Fortunately for Nanjones, it is not in that situation. Its production-volume variance is favorable.

explanations.A: This is the fixed overhead spending variance, not the fixed overhead production-volume variance. The fixed overhead spending variance is the difference between actual fixed overhead incurred for the month (given as $101,200) and budgeted fixed overhead for the month (given as $100,000). Since it is positive, it is unfavorable. The fixed overhead production-volume variance is the difference between the budgeted amount of fixed overhead and the amount of fixed overhead applied (standard rate × standard input for the actual level of output). We already said that the budgeted fixed overhead is given as $100,000. The amount applied must be calculated from the information given. The amount of fixed overhead applied is the application rate per machine hour multiplied by the number of machine hours allowed for the actual output. The application rate per machine hour is the annual budgeted fixed overhead divided by the annual number of machine hours planned to be used.
explanations.B: The fixed overhead production-volume variance is the difference between the budgeted amount of fixed overhead and the amount of fixed overhead applied (standard rate × standard input for the actual level of output). If in the calculation of fixed manufacturing overhead applied the static budget amount of machine hours (22,000) were used, we would come up with an amount of $110,000 FOH applied. And the fixed overhead volume variance would be $10,000 ($110,000 − $100,000) favorable; which is incorrect. In the calculation of fixed overhead applied, we should use the number of standard machine hours for the actual level of output (21,000 hours). See the correct answer for a complete explanation and information on interpreting this variance.
explanations.C: This answer is the amount of applied fixed overhead minus the budgeted fixed overhead. The fixed overhead production-volume variance is the budgeted amount of fixed overhead minus the amount of fixed overhead applied (standard rate × standard input for the actual level of output). This is the only time for an expense variance calculation that a budgeted cost amount comes before an actual cost amount, and yet a negative amount is a favorable variance. A negative amount, meaning the amount of fixed overhead applied was greater than the budgeted amount, is favorable because it means the facilities were used more than was planned, which is good.

The term does not specify whether it is a cost per unit or a total cost, and if a total cost, whether it is a static budget amount or a flexible budget amount. explanations.B: This is the definition of the total variable overhead variance. question: A company that consistently underapplies fixed overhead in its standard cost system will report a(n)

options.A: unfavorable fixed overhead efficiency variance.
options.B: unfavorable total fixed overhead variance.
options.C: favorable fixed overhead spending variance.
options.D: favorable fixed overhead production-volume variance.

correctExplanation: A company that consistently underapplies fixed overhead in its standard cost system will report an unfavorable total fixed overhead variance. The total fixed overhead variance is the combination of the fixed overhead spending variance and the fixed overhead production-volume variance. The fixed overhead spending variance is actual fixed overhead incurred minus budgeted fixed overhead, The fixed overhead production-volume variance is budgeted fixed overhead minus fixed overhead applied. Therefore, the total fixed overhead variance is actual fixed overhead incurred minus fixed overhead applied. An under-application of fixed overhead will cause an unfavorable total fixed overhead variance because actual fixed overhead incurred will be greater than fixed overhead applied.

explanations.A: There is no such thing as a fixed overhead efficiency variance, because fixed manufacturing costs do not have any relation to levels of output as long as the output remains in the relevant range and therefore cannot be used either efficiently or inefficiently. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.C: The fixed overhead spending variance is actual fixed overhead incurred minus budgeted fixed overhead. Overhead applied is not a part of the calculation of the fixed overhead spending variance, so it cannot affect it. Please see the correct answer explanation for more information.
explanations.D: The fixed overhead production-volume variance is budgeted fixed overhead minus fixed overhead applied. A favorable fixed overhead production-volume variance would be caused by an actual level of production that is higher than the budgeted level of production. If actual production is higher than budgeted production, fixed overhead will be over-applied, not under-applied.

intro: Franklin Products has an estimated practical capacity of 90,000 machine hours, and each unit requires two machine hours. The following data apply to a recent accounting period.
table: Budgeted variable overhead at 90,000 machine hours
tail: Of the following factors, Franklin Products' production-volume variance is most likely to have been caused by

options.A: a wage hike granted to a production supervisor after the budget was finalized.
options.B: temporary employment of workers with lower skill levels than originally anticipated.
options.C: acceptance of an unexpected sales order.
options.D: a newly imposed initiative to reduce finished goods inventory levels.

correctExplanation: The fixed overhead production volume variance is Budgeted Fixed Overhead − Fixed Overhead Applied. The FOH production-volume variance is $30,000 unfavorable because actual production of 42,000 units was lower than budgeted production of 45,000 units (calculated as practical capacity of 90,000 MH divided by 2 standard MH allowed per unit). The FOH application rate was $450,000 budgeted FOH divided by 90,000 MH = $5/MH. FOH applied was 42,000 units actually produced × 2 MH allowed/unit × $5/MH = $420,000. The FOH production-volume variance was $450,000 budgeted FOH − $420,000 FOH applied = $30,000 Unfavorable. A newly imposed initiative (imposed after the budget was finalized) to reduce finished goods inventory would cause actual production to be lower than budgeted production, leading to the unfavorable FOH production-volume variance.

explanations.A: The fixed overhead production-volume variance is Budgeted Fixed Overhead − Fixed Overhead Applied. Although the compensation paid production supervisors is included in fixed manufacturing overhead, a wage hike granted to a production supervisor after the budget was finalized would not change the FOH production-volume variance because it would not change budgeted FOH. While it would change actual FOH incurred which would affect the FOH spending variance, it would not affect the FOH production-volume variance because actual FOH incurred is not used in the calculation of the production-volume variance.
explanations.B: The fixed overhead production volume variance is Budgeted Fixed Overhead − Fixed Overhead Applied. Actual production that is lower than budgeted production will cause an unfavorable FOH production volume variance. Temporary employment of workers with lower skill levels than originally anticipated can cause an unfavorable direct material quantity (usage) variance, but it would not ordinarily cause actual production to be lower than planned production. Therefore, this is not the best answer choice for the question.
explanations.C: The fixed overhead production-volume variance is Budgeted Fixed Overhead − Fixed Overhead Applied. Acceptance of an unexpected sales order would not change either budgeted fixed overhead or fixed overhead applied, so it would not affect the FOH production volume variance.

question: For a given time period, a company had a favorable material quantity variance, a favorable direct labor efficiency variance, and a favorable fixed overhead volume variance. Of the following, the one factor that could not have caused all three variances is

options.A: the purchase of more efficient machinery.
options.B: the purchase of higher quality materials.
options.C: the use of lower-skilled workers.
options.D: an increase in production supervision.

correctExplanation: The use of lower-skilled workers could not be a cause of these three favorable variances. Lower-skilled employees will make more mistakes than highly-skilled employees. That will result in more materials being used than the standard (an unfavorable direct material quantity variance). It will also result in a greater amount of direct labor time required than the standard (an unfavorable direct labor efficiency variance). And it will result in an unfavorable fixed overhead production-volume variance, because lower-skilled employees would require more time to produce each unit. In addition, a greater number of units would be rejected as defective. Both of these would lead to a lower production volume than was planned which creates an unfavorable fixed overhead production-volume variance.

explanations.A: The purchase of more efficient machinery could cause all three variances. Use of more efficient machinery could lead to a favorable material quantity variance if less direct materials were ruined in production due to better machinery being used. The purchase of more efficient machinery could also lead to a favorable direct labor efficiency variance, because employees would be able to produce more units of finished goods when the machinery they are using is more efficient. question: If overhead is applied on the basis of units of the activity base actually used for the actual output, the variable overhead efficiency variance will be:
